subtopic: THE PRIME MINISTER-PRESS REPORT OP SPEECH OF MR. PEARKES IN VANCOUVER

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THE PRIME MINISTER-PRESS REPORT OP SPEECH OF MR. PEARKES IN VANCOUVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege concerning a matter which is in the nature of a reflection upon myself as an hon. member of this house and as Prime Minister and which I think might well be resented as an indignity against the house itself. I refer to a report of a speech that was made by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) which appears in the Vancouver Daily Province of Wednesday, March 31, 1948. The heading is, "Pearkes claims Mackenzie ousted over pensions". The article is by Gordon McCallum and it reads:
A Canadian war hero member of parliament charged Tuesday night that Right Honourable Ian Mackenzie was ousted from the cabinet because he rowed with Prime Minister King over the size of veterans pensions.
Major-General G. R. Pearkes, V.C., Conservative member of parliament for Nanaimo, told a Vancouver Centre Conservative nomination meeting: "Your member fought to get a better increase in pensions than the Prime Minister would authorize. His reward was, Thank you. Now get out. You will go to the senate. I will get my former private secretary in your place.' I will defy anyone to contradict that this is what happened."
I say to the hon. member for Nanaimo that I contradict his statement wholly and completely; there is not one word of truth in it from beginning to end. The circumstances under which Mr. Mackenzie tendered his resignation and which led to my recommending His Excellency to appoint him to the senate appear in an exchange of correspondence that took place between us and which is published in Hansard of Monday, January 26, 1948.
At no time have I had a word of difference with the former minister of veterans affairs over any questions relating to pensions for returned soldiers. Indeed I think the former minister will say that he had not a stronger supporter than myself in all the legislation which he brought forward during the time he was in office to improve the condition of the war veterans.
As for the selection of the Liberal candidate in the constituency, I let it be known publicly that I wished to have nothing whatever to do directly or indirectly with directing the choice by the Liberal convention of the candidate who was to contest that riding. I did not seek to influence, nor did I influence either directly or indirectly, the choice of the convention when it selected Mr. Campney as the candidate.

subtopic: DEEPSEA SHIPOWNERS AND DECK, ENGINEER AND WIRELESS OPERATORS-UNION PROPOSALS FOR ARBITRATION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: DEEPSEA SHIPOWNERS AND DECK, ENGINEER AND WIRELESS OPERATORS-UNION PROPOSALS FOR ARBITRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Labour. He said in reply to a question I asked him on March 24, regarding the union proposals for arbitration

Inquiries of the Ministry
in the seamen's strike, that he was awaiting a reply from the shipowners. Can the minister now tell the house what is the attitude of the shipowners to the arbitration proposal?

subtopic: DEEPSEA SHIPOWNERS AND DECK, ENGINEER AND WIRELESS OPERATORS-UNION PROPOSALS FOR ARBITRATION
speechtext:
My hon. friend is in error in referring to it as the seamen's strike. It is a strike of the deck, engineer and wireless officers. I have a statement on the position at the moment which I shall now give to the house.
In reply to the question of the hon. member for Vancouver East, members will recall that all issues in dispute between the two federations representing deepsea shipowners on the east and west coasts and the three unions representing the licensed deck, engineer and wireless officers of their Canadian-registered ships were fully considered by Mr. Justice D. A. McNiven, of Regina, acting as an industrial disputes inquiry commissioner.
In spite of his patient and painstaking efforts, the commissioner was unable to secure a settlement of the dispute and submitted his report to the Minister of Labour on January 22.
The recommendations made by the commissioner were used as the basis of further direct negotiations, which took place between the parties at Vancouver during February. These direct negotiations broke down early in March, at which time the shipowners announced that they were putting into immediate effect all of the recommendations of Mr. Justice McNiven except two, which involved the payment of an overtime allowance to radio officers and the deck and engineer officers' security watch abroad. The officers' unions held out for the adoption of all of the commissioners' recommendations, together with overtime pay on an hourly rather than a lump sum basis, "pro rata" leave in connection with annual vacations with pay, and other concessions.
A strike was called on March 3 upon all ocean-going dry cargo vessels touching Canadian ports, and up to date about thirty-two vessels have been immobilized.
Subsequently, both sides to the dispute sought the assistance of the Department of Labour and everything possible has been done to bring the parties into agreement. Various arbitration proposals were put forward from union sources, and on March 25 the Minister of Labour formally suggested to the shipping operators that they authorize him to approach the unions with an offer of an immediate return to work by the officers conditional upon acceptance of the employers' Vancouver offer of March 1, together with arbitration of the questions of hourly overtime pay and pro rata
leave. This was done in the belief that the suggestion was capable of bringing about an early settlement, and that it was not unreasonable since it was felt that the two points on which arbitration was proposed were rather minor ones.
On March 31 the two federations of shipowners informed the Minister of Labour that they were now prepared to accept the recommendations of Mr. Justice McNiven in their entirety providing the ships' officers now on strike did likewise and returned to work forthwith, and provided that the provisions of the commissioners' recommendations should remain in effect until January 31, 1949. The owners were not prepared to arbitrate any issues not recommended for adoption by the commissioner.
With regard to a suggestion by the unions that all officers should be reinstated without discrimination and that those on articles should not be penalized under the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act, the operators maintained that they should not be asked to condone what they described as the illegal actions of officers who had broken their articles of agreement.
I should add here that one of the twenty-six companies involved in the dispute, the Federal Commerce and Navigation Company Limited, with the assistance of the department reached an agreement with its employees which has been endorsed by the unions concerned, and I had word from the company this morning that its "ships sailed over the week-end".
This single settlement provides that all of Mr. Justice McNiven's recommendations will be implemented; that final and binding arbitration will take place on the questions of hourly overtime pay and pro rata leave; and that so far as the Federal Commerce and Navigation Company can influence the matter, there shall be no penalization of officers under the Canada Shipping Act, and the company will not discriminate against its employees for having engaged in strike action.
Assurances have been received from two of the officers' unions, namely, the Canadian Merchant Service Guild and the National Association of Marine Engineers, that if the east and west coast shipowners will agree to the same terms as the Federal Commerce and Navigation Company, the strike will be terminated immediately.
The latest word from the shipowners' federations, received on Saturday, is that they are not prepared to go beyond their offer of March 31, and that they consider their "final position ' to be in the long-term public
Inquiries oj the Ministry

interest. They also submitted that their willingness now to accept in full the recommendations of the commissioner absolved them from any suggestion of being unreasonable or arbitrary in refusing to accept arbitration of other issues which were fully considered by Mr. Justice McNiven and which, if conceded, might endanger the competitive position of Canada's merchant marine.
The principal recommendations contained in the commissioner's report were that:-
1.	The basic wages of officers holding certificates should be increased by from $20 to $25 per month-and, in the case of deck and engineer officers who have completed certain periods of continuous and satisfactory service with the same company, increases up to $35 per month should be granted.
2.	Stipulated lump-sum amounts of overtime pay should be paid to deck, engineer and radio officers as compensation for all work performed in addition to watch-keeping duties.
3.	Longer vacations with pay should be granted.
4.	Compensation should be made for loss of personal effects in the event of marine disaster.
5.	Allowances should be made for deck and engineer officers' security watches abroad.
6.	Concessions as to wages and annual leave should be made retroactive to October 15, 1947.
7.	No concessions should be granted in respect of union security beyond the existing recognition of the unions concerned as sole bargaining agents for licensed officers, coupled with the preferential hiring of union members.

subtopic: EMERGENCY PAYMENTS TO ASSIST IN MEETING INCREASED COST OF PRODUCTION

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, December 19, 1947, consideration of the motion of Mr. Abbott for the second reading of Bill No. 7, respecting emergency payments to assist in meeting increased cost of production of gold.

subtopic: EMERGENCY PAYMENTS TO ASSIST IN MEETING INCREASED COST OF PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the radio broadcast made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on November 17 he announced a policy of bonus-ing the gold mines in order to assist them in the difficult days through which they were passing, and in that broadcast the amount of $7 was the figure which it was proposed at that time to give by way of bonus to the mines. Owing to objections of officials at Washington, however, this was changed and a new scheme of bonusing was brought down, as contained in this bill.
The gold mining industry as a whole is opposed to being bonused, for the simple reason that it makes them the creature of the government and possibly allows the government in days to come to interfere with the management and with the manner in which the business is to be carried on.
The bonus that is now being considered in this bill is in my opinion of some help to the industry but it is not of any great assistance. Most of the mining companies have already passed this bonus on to their labour, for from January 1 the increase in wages in Ontario and

Gold Mining
Quebec has more than absorbed the total amount of the bonus payable under this bill.
Many discussions have taken place regarding the state of the gold mining industry and it was only during the last session when this matter was before the house that I brought certain aspects of the situation to the attention of the Minister of Finance, and I remember that on one occasion he stated that I was talking for Bay Street. However, I was glad that in November the government had come to realize that the industry was in a very unsatisfactory condition and that it was necessary for the government to give it some assistance.
Some of the gold mining companies have suggested various plans, one of which was of course the free marketing of gold. I am not going to talk about that today. My only point is that there may be some place in the world where some or all of our gold can be sold at a price higher than $35 and the proceeds from these sales converted into United States dollars, and the excess paid to the producer.
The troubles of the industry started in 1946 on the day when parity was brought about by the government in arbitrarily placing the Canadian dollar on a parity with that of the United States. I have said before that the industry did not want this bonus. It was not their idea but the idea of the government, and the industry feels that this bonus is being given at this time to make up in some small degree for the placing of our money on a parity with that of the United States.
I think at this time I should say something about the industry itself. Many people, and especially members to my left, seem to think that only a few wealthy shareholders of producing gold mines are the ones who will benefit by any bill such as that which is before us at this time. In this connection it might be pointed out that there are from 250,000 to 300,000 registered shareholders of Canadian mines, and one has only to look at the shareholders list to see the size of the blocks of shares. One company of which I have some knowledge has approximately 8,000 shareholders of whom there are only a few hundred having more than 500 shares of stock, the majority of the shareholders holding less than 100 or 200 shares.
I bring this question up now because I am of -the opinion that this bill is quite necessary at this time so that the industry may at least get some help from the government to carry them on the road to recovery. Probably few members, and few people in this country, have a knowledge of the broad effect of our gold 5849-170J
mines on the Canadian economy. It is too early to give many figures for the year 1947, but I have one or two figures here with regard to purchases and expenditures of some of the Canadian mines. I would take as an example the Sigma mines operating in the Bourlamaque area of the province of Quebec. Last year they made purchases from 353 individual suppliers in 96 different municipalities. The Noranda mines during the year 1947 paid for operating supplies $12,420,000, for freight and transportation $1,150,000 and for hydro power $1,012,000. Approximately 96 per cent of the total expenditures of Noranda and its subsidiaries was spent in Canada, and these orders were distributed to 1,200 firms, providing employment for men and women living in 140 Canadian towns and cities.
Two of the corporation's comparatively small subsidiaries accounted for approximately $600,000 worth of supplies, which included such items as metal products, equipment, explosives, lumber and timber, reagents and chemicals, electrical equipment and supplies, air operated equipment and parts, pipe and fittings, fuel, petroleum products, rubber products, paints, and a great variety of other items.
It may interest hon. members of the house to know some of the communities which benefited from these purchases. The principal communities in Ontario, for instance, were Amherstburg, Baden, Belleville, Blind River, Bowmanville, Brampton, Brockville, Cobalt! Cooksville, Dundas, Eganville, Fort Erie, Galt, Gananoque, Niagara Falls, Peterborough, and many others. In Quebec the purchases were made at such places as Beloeil, Joliette, Sorel, Lachine, La Tuque, Montreal, Rock Island, and Shawinigan Falls.
I have given these figures to show what this industry means not only to the people who work in the mines but to those who work in the factories that supply the necessary tools and equipment to keep the mines going. Then on top of that, with the millions of dollars paid out in wages, there is the great purchasing power built up by the workers for such things as clothes, furniture and other household effects that have to be purchased by the people living in the mining districts. Point number two is that consideration should be given by the department to the matter of setting up a general welfare plan in the community for the purpose of building up the morale of the workers in their homes and raising their standards, and recognizing them as human beings. If you are going to spend the taxpayers' money to get production, the man

I have listened to the leaders of the C.C.F. and the Social Credit party in their arguments that subsidies are being paid for gold but no subsidies for foodstuffs. I think we are overlooking this one fact. This industry is nationalized. I doubt whether the gold mines themselves would be interested in a subsidy for their product if they had a free market for their gold; but when you nationalize an industry and determine that there is only one source through which the product can be marketed, and the price is set by the purchaser, then I feel that the subsidy is indeed justified.
I am not greatly impressed by the criticism which is offered with respect to the position taken by the Progressive Conservative party in relation to the subsidy on gold. May I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that gold has been accepted as a standard of value since the days of the Egyptians; and all down through the ages the countries which had the gold were the leaders in commerce and in industry. It has been accepted as a precious metal, durable and convertible into the things which we need. Canada has been particularly blessed. We have vast resources of this very precious metal. Unfortunately some of our mines are what is referred to as sub-marginal. That gold in the rock is of very little value to mankind unless it can be mined or taken from the rock. It does seem unusual-yet it is true-that we should exhaust our energies and devote our time and talent and labour to the development or the mining of ore simply to store it in a vault. But that has been the accepted practice, particularly since gold has been nationalized and is used more or less as a monetary basis, irrespective of the fact that we are not on what we call a gold standard. Nevertheless it has a fixed value.
It is interesting to note that in Soviet Russia they are building up huge gold reserves; just how great, we do not know. But we do know that they have put a value upon gold possibly greater than any other commodity which they are able to use, inasmuch as they do know that the gold is exchangeable for all the other products which we desire. As a matter of fact I suppose if one were to delve into history he would find that we would never have had the so-called monetary system or the system of bank notes had it not been for gold.
Historians will tell you that in the early days when people carried their gold with them in little cubes, exchanges were made by barter and trade, and the difference was adjusted

by paring or slicing off a piece of gold from one man's gold nugget and tamping it on to the other until the better traders presently found themselves with a volume of gold which was very difficult to carry about with them. Gold is a very heavy metal. I believe a fourteen-inch cube of gold weighs in the neighbourhood of one ton. So the next thing was to find a place to store the gold, and the logical place was with the goldsmith, the man who was making gold into beautiful ornaments, gold cloth and other materials which were in demand in those early days. By and by there came a time when a man had a certain amount of gold stored and it was generally understood that he had this gold, so that instead of adjusting his balance by paring off from his gold block and handing that to the other fellow, he simply issued an order on the goldsmith. As long as that order he had issued over his signature was accepted as genuine, the scrip, so to speak, was used just as we use our dollar bills or bank notes today, and it rvas passed on from one person to another and so made the free medium of exchange. That continued so long as there was confidence that the gold was there. That w'as the beginning of our monetary system.
Whether our monetary system has been good or bad, it has served a useful purpose all through the ages, and I for one have only one criticism to offer. I will go along with the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), that there should be set up certain parts of the bonus for the benefit of the miners who dig the ore, provided the bonus is offered straight across the board.
I cannot understand why we should undertake a measure of this kind, which appears so complicated on the face of it. Someone in days gone by used the term "too little and too late". It could be said that this measure is too confusing and too difficult of administration. It will lead to another great army of employees -I was going to use the word "bureaucrats", but that is being overplayed. At any rate it will lead to the employment of officials who must go from place to place, check with the mines, determine their production for the basic period and determine the bonus to which they are entitled.
I believe the minister was on the right track in his first approach to the problem. Just what Washington had to do with it, what right they had to interfere, is difficult for me to understand. I believe it was understood that we were setting up a free market for gold, or a market for gold in which we were paying more for gold than the United States. It was not clearly understood that our bonus was for native-mined gold whereby we could

Gold Mining
stimulate the production and discovery of gold mines and the extraction of the precious metal from the rock. Had that been made clear it could have been accepted as a sound practice, inasmuch as it was an admission at the time, irrespective of the position the government took on the question of the parity of our dollar with that of the United States, that our dollar was not worth the amount of the United States dollar. It should have been understood that we were simply seeking to offset that condition and to encourage the production of a commodity with great quantities of which we have been blessed.
As a matter of fact, Canada should be in the first rank of the world's gold producers. It is true that we stand well up in comparison with other countries, but I would urge, and urge constantly, that every effort be made to give an incentive to those who are willing to go into the hinterland on prospecting tours to discover mines, and we should encourage capitalists or investors, in other words the public, to risk their capital in the development of the mines.
Our hon. friends to the left would have you believe that they can designate certain mines which indeed have made a success and are now returning substantial dividends to those who were willing to take a chance and invest their money, which was risk capital. But all you have to do is to pick up a mining handbook and read the names of hundreds upon hundreds of companies who received a degree of public support, raising millions of dollars for the development of gold mines, but were more or less a failure.
I believe it was Mark Twain who said that a mine is a hole in the ground with a large cover at the top. It would appear that in many mines an effort was made to secure risk capital and to develop these ventures, but they had little chance from the beginning. And yet that old incentive, that desire to discover some shortcut to fortune, is inherent in everyone who is at all human. We all like to feel that we have an opportunity to enrich ourselves without expending too much energy or too much labour in the accomplishment. The hon. member for Cape Breton South said that plans are made for the development of these mines and that they know where they are going. I doubt if that can be accepted as a fact, because, after all, all the veins are not visible on the surface of the rock. As the shaft is deepened and the tunnels made, crosscuts are made to discover other veins which might be below the surface. Diamond drills, of course, have made a tremendous contribu-5849-171-i
tion to the task and to the advantages which we have not heretofore enjoyed in the discovery of mines.
I say to the minister that we should not pick and choose. Whatever we are going to do for the gold mining industry should be done across the board. If we are prepared to pay $40 an ounce for native-mined gold we should not allow pressure from any source to prevent us from developing our own rich resources which we possess as a gift from God. We should encourage our people to take the chance to develop something which is accepted today as the standard of value and which will secure the very things we need most. In other words, so long as we have a good reserve of gold we need not worry a great deal about our position in relation to the United States dollar.
If we are to produce gold, and it is there to be produced, if we can store it against our foreign trade balances, and if we can seek to develop trade with those who are willing to trade with us, I am sure the situation in relation to the United States will in time adjust itself.
As a closing thought I again remind the house that we are confused in any criticism we offer with respect to the bonusing of gold if we overlook the fact that in 1932 the late President Roosevelt on becoming President of the United States nationalized gold, and since that time the gold clause has been removed from their bonds and from their currency. No longer do they promise to pay in gold. Since that time gold has had a fixed value but has had only one definite fixed market, one purchaser, and that is the national purchaser.
Because of that restriction, I say that the subsidy is justified. Otherwise, if we are not prepared to pay it and we wish to put gold in the same position as the commodities to which my hon. friends have referred, then let us remove the restrictions, let the gold miners dispose of their product as they will, and they will not seek the subsidy, because gold is in great demand today. It is one of the most durable metals in the world. We should give every incentive to those who are willing to take a chance to develop this rich natural resource, and we should either pay the subsidy straight across the board or forget all about it and let the gold miners market their product where they wish to.

speechtext:
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that I must say something with respect to this Bill No. 7, which is virtually to subsidize the production of gold. As the leader of this 'party has already said, conditions are as they are; and we must deal with circumstances as they are, not with circumstances as we
Gold Mining

should like them to be. The fact of the matter remains that, through government policy, we have been driven to a place where we are short of some other nation's dollars and that, in order to build up our United States credits, it is found necessary to endeavour to export gold to that country. It seems a little bit difficult to oppose a measure which would aid in exporting one ounce of gold in return for $35 or $37 worth of goods. But I am wondering if there is not a principle involved, namely, that if we resort to the export of gold in order that we may import real wealth, we may not find ourselves in a position at some future time where we shall be asked to accept imports of gold in payment for the export of our real wealth.
I cannot help feeling that there is a vital principle involved in this bill; that there is not merely the fact that the government desires to subsidize the production of gold in order to get a higher production, but that there is the principle whereby this country is forced to bow down and pay obeisance to the golden gods of mammon. That to my mind is a most important principle.
The leader of this group has protested the fact that, while it may appear to be necessary to subsidize the production of gold, evidently it has not appeared necessary for the government to subsidize the more important industries. During the Easter recess, on my visit to my constituency, many people, particularly farmers, came to me almost unanimously sounding one note, namely that through the present financial policy of the government their production, production from the land, was actually being sabotaged; that the farmers were being driven into a position where it would not pay them to produce the abundance of foodstuffs which this and other countries need. I believe the dangerous principle underlying this bill is that we are to subsidize the production of what I term a fictitious metal, while at the same time we sabotage the production of real wealth in this countiy. That, I say again, is an extremely important principle.
Let us remember that the land of a country is the life-blood of that nation. A nation cannot exist unless it eats, and the only place from which we get food is the land, through agriculture. A nation cannot live except it be clothed, and the only place from which we get our clothing is the land. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott)1 may be wearing a suit that is all wool and a yard wide. If so, some poor sheep had to give its fleece before he could get that suit of clothes; and

that sheep could not exist except it grazed on the land. Yet during the war we paid farmers to stop producing! Perhaps the Minister of Finance is wearing a nice pair of shoes.

speechtext:
Yes, but the fact of the matter is that we are not in heaven yet; we are still on the ground. Even though the Minister of Finance may have his head in the clouds, our feet are still on the ground. I claim that bowing down to a system which requires a fictitious metal to keep it going, while at the same time we penalize the production of real wealth, is a crime against civilization and a sin against the Creator who makes the earth green, who sends the rain and the sunshine in their season to produce for us that by which the people live. That is the principle; and there is no question but that today the farmer is being penalized for producing.
I do not want to get off on another subject, but I know that right now the farmers are making out their income tax forms. Our

Gold Mining
present policy of taxation penalizes the production of real wealth. The more a man produces, the more he should be paid, but that is not the way it operates. Our present bungling financial policy means that the more a farmer produces, the more he has taken from him. It is the same with the coal miner. He works so many days producing the coal that keeps industry going and warms our homes; but he is penalized if he puts in overtime, so he does not work even full time. That system is wrong.
Let us put first things first. If I remember correctly-and I am trusting to my recollection of Napoleonic history-I believe it was Napoleon who once said the most important thing in civilization was agriculture, and it should be put first; the second most important thing was manufacturing, while the third and least important was financial policy. I believe Napoleon was right in that diagnosis, but somehow or another present governments have reversed that order.
The first thing, which is all important, is financial policy. Next are manufacturing and the secondary industries, while the third and last of the three in importance is agriculture. That is wrong, and the present policy in Canada is wrong. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that if we subsidize the production of a fictitious metal and at the same time penalize the production of real wealth, that is a sin; and I say to the present Minister of Finance and his colleagues, be sure your sin will find you out. It is beginning to find us out now. A few years ago we had the Bretton Woods agreement up for consideration. We in this corner argued that this agreement virtually put us back upon the gold standard. Well, what has happened? That agreement is partly responsible for the present austerity program. Be sure your sins will find you out; and whatsoever a man soweth that shall he also reap. That is a divine law which no one can repudiate or get around. If we sow the seeds of idol worship of the golden gods of mammon, then in due season we shall reap that which we deserve.
Let us make sure we give our agricultural industry all possible encouragement to produce everything it can. The hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Case) spoke of the advisability of producing this gold and putting it in a storehouse. I am not going to argue particularly against that, but let me say this. A few years ago we spoke of the production of foodstuffs in this country, and we in this corner-I would refer especially to the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blaclcmore), who made a passionate plea-asked for the production and storage of vast quantities of foodstuffs against the coming of a possible evil day. Did we do that?
We did not. We paid our farmers to stop producing. That principle is wrong.
So I say, Mr. Speaker, that we have to get right back to the real, fundamental principles. The greatest wealth of this country is in its actual production of the means of life. Instead of penalizing and discouraging that, we should encourage it all we can by the payment of subsidies, if possible, and by the removal of this terrible system of taxation. We should put first things first and see that things are kept in their proper place. That is my plea today. It may seem strange that, after a speech such as I have delivered, we should say we will support the bill. We are only doing that by reason of the fact that the government, through its bungling financial policy, has driven this country into such a position that, at least for the time being, we may be able to offset part of our foreign debts, shall I say, by this simple method. It will help for the time being. I say once again that if the government are absolutely bent on driving this country back to a fictitious monetary standard such as gold, some day we shall reap the reward of our evil ways.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is possible for anyone who lives in the Thunder Bay district or in northern Ontario not to be interested in gold mining. I have the finest regard for the gold mining experts in our country. During the depression many of our young men could get only So a month in the relief camps, but a great number of young married men were employed by the gold mining industry in our district.
If this bill will do anything to steady that industry, it will be a good thing. It is not altogether true that you dig gold out of one hole and put it in another. That is a fine statement, but in order for a statement to carry weight it must be true. The other day I assisted a young man to place a ring upon the left finger of his intended when they cemented their friendship for life. I think that is a good use for gold. The jewelry business is the backbone of our gold industry. As I say, if this bill does nothing more than steady the industry that we know a little about I think we should support it absolutely.
I should like to offer a suggestion to the minister and I know he is big enough to take a suggestion from a small individual. The prospectors who do the hard work get very little for it as compared with the mining magnates. These prospectors should have some encouragement. I suggest that when they make a find and report it to the department of mines or to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and
Gold Mining

experts are sent in, if it is found to be all right after drilling, after the mine is opened up, then the mining industry or those interested should pay back to the government what it costs. That is not a subsidy, is it? I think this bill will do a little bit. As the Scotch say to us, many a mickle makes a muckle.
Mr. HARRY R. JACKMAN (Rosedale): Mr. Speaker, several hon. members have spoken on the possibility of improving the lot of the miner. That is a suggestion which I think will find ready acceptance in all parts of this house. As we know, the miner's lot is not an easy one, but on the other hand I know that in the gold mines which I have visited it seemed to be an interesting occupation and the miners underground seemed to take just as much interest in it as the geologists and engineers above ground. May I point out that in order to provide better conditions it is necessary to make the industry healthy and this bill will provide some little help to a large part of the mining industry.
We find the highest industrial standards in the United States and Canada because those countries are the most prosperous industrially and commercially. Where you have prosperity, in due course you have a higher standard of working conditions and living. I was glad to hear not long ago hon. members of the C.C.F. party say that they knew of no country in which they would rather live than in our own Canada.
While it is true that a good many of us in this house are against subsidies in principle, nevertheless there are times when in order to keep an industry alive a subsidy or some assistance such as is given under this bill is necessary. May I point out that the gold mining industry is somewhat different from any other industry in this country in that it is to a large extent, if not 100 per cent, an export industry. For reasons which I shall give later, that is a matter of some importance.
I should like to know from the minister in charge of this bill the government's long-term policy with regard to gold mining in this country. To use the vernacular, the measure before the house is nothing more than a shot in the arm. It will perhaps keep the industry going for a while; but with rising costs occurring almost daily, whether it be in the field of materials or in the field of labour, this small measure of assistance may be quickly lost to the mines and they will be in the same position and in the same plight as they were before the government gave consideration to providing some aid. It would be interesting to know just why the government is giving this aid of which we are all so much in favour. Does the

government intend to adopt a further policy if necessary, or what is the real policy of the government in regard to the gold mining industry?
Gold production in Canada in 1939 amounted to $184,000,000, and in 1941 it had increased to $205,000,000. This was quite a substantial boost, and it was at a time when those in charge of the gold mining industry were doing everything they could to carry out the government's request and make as great a contribution as possible to the war effort by producing as much gold or as much foreign exchange as possible. They produced gold even to the extent of taking high-grade ore which would ordinarily have been used over a period of years and forgoing certain development work which they would ordinarily have undertaken and which would have used manpower which was otherwise used in direct production.
By 1946 we find that gold production had fallen from the $205,000,000 peak during the war to $104,000,000. Production was just about cut in half. When the final figures are available for 1947 I think it will be found that production has been cut in two, to say the least. This may be partly due to government action.
For the benefit of those who may be interested, may I say that during the war I was not a strenuous advocate of increased production of gold because we needed manpower in other fields so urgently. Yet our gold did provide a means of purchasing war materials, in particular from the United States. After the United States joined us, I was not one of those who encouraged production. I merely want to belie any feeling anyone might conceivably have that I am primarily interested in gold stocks per se; I am interested in the welfare of Canada as a whole.
I should like to draw the attention of the house to the statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) during the debate on the excise tax bill when he was refuting any suggestion from- this side of the house that we might have been better off had the government not followed its policy of July 5, 1946, of up-valuating our dollar to a parity with that of the United States dollar. Referring to that time, I find that the minister said on January 30 of this year, as reported at page 735 of Hansard:
In my judgment, inability to export is the only real justification for currency depreciation on the part of any country.
We have in the gold mining industry one of our basic industries; or rather I should1 like to know whether the government considers it a basic industry or even an important industry.

Gold Mining
We have a product there, namely gold, which we cannot sell abroad because our internal costs in the industry are too high. This obviously
is an example which refutes the minister's suggestion that Canada is in a position to sell abroad so far as costs are concerned, for our internal costs in the gold mining industry in this country are so high that we cannot sell gold at the world price, which is apparently the only price that is available.
One of the difficulties in having a reasonable price for gold at the present time or of having a price which gives us a fair return on this precious metal is that rock which would normally be commercial is passed over because the price is too low to make its extraction commercially justifiable.
It is perhaps also worth mentioning that there are many people, if not the great majority, in Canada who would rather see a certain -amount of premium, let us say ten per cent, paid for gold under certain circumstances. They would be quite willing to pay that premium, apart altogether from any action which the government might -take, and thus save themselves from the extraordinary penalty which the Minister of Finance has imposed on the people by putting into force these very unpopular excise taxes of 25 per cent and more. If gold were produced we would have more exchange and we would- not have to suffer the heavy and extraordinarily inconvenient burden and the inequities which the new excise taxes impose upon us at the present time.
One sometimes wonders, Mr. Speaker, when one realizes that Bretton Woods or the international monetary fund has to be consulted at every turn we take, even to help a domestic industry, whether we listened as carefully as we might have done to some of our Social Credit friends who pointed out that we were giving up a substantial part of our sovereignty when we became a member of the international monetary fund. The government's first proposal to give some assistance to the gold mining industry had to be withdrawn, apparently because it could not pass muster with the governors of the international monetary fund, and- the present proposal might have been quite otherwise than it is, for all the house knows, and the government might have been willing to go farther, had not its proposal eventually to go again before the international monetary fund to see whether it was satisfactory to its governors.
In this connection I should like to say a word in favour of the free coinage of gold. I do not know what the opinion of the international monetary fund is in regard to that, although I suspect it is opposed, but there are many people in this country who would like
to be able to purchase gold even at a premium if necessary. This leads me to say a word or two to belie the suggestion that gold is purely a fictitious commodity with no real value. As long as people are willing to pay for gold and to give for it other goods in exchange, as are the United States and every other country in the world, gold has a very real value. There is no use in considering moral values in this particular case any more than there is in any other case. One might just as well point to articles of clothing and food and drink as having no particular value; in fact some might claim that some of these commodities were injurious. Yet we go on producing them. Gold will always have great value as long as people in the world are willing to exchange other things for it. It will have great value I think long after many of the currencies which today are considered of value have passed into the limbo of forgotten things. So I suggest to the government that if they want to do more for the gold mining industry it would be quite possible to allow the free coinage of gold and let people who wish to have it store up gold for a day which they cannot foresee but which perhaps they can envisage when they believe that gold will afford them a protection which perhaps no other commodity or form of security can give. It would also be anti-inflationary if we allowed the free coinage of gold, because gold need not then come into the monetary system as a basis for credit extension.
I do want to emphasize before this bill passes, and on this side I think we shall give support to it, that the government should tell the house exactly what its policy is in regard to the important industry of gold mining in Canada. I do not wish the Minister of Finance to quibble with me and say that the policy of the government is embodied in this little bill before us, because it is a very small measure as he well knows. It is, as I said before, a shot in the arm which perhaps will enable the industry to carry on for a little while, but as he knows there are many indications on the horizon of squalls and tempests in the way of rising costs which might easily upset the industry and set it back further than it was at the time when he first gave consideration to this bill.
My hon. friend the member for York South (Mr. Cockeram) has already pointed out the great value to Canada of the gold mining industry and its affiliated and dependent industries. It is a crucial industry in Canada and it is in a critical position at the present time. Therefore I ask the government to state what its long-term policy is with regard to this vital industry.

The first is the number of people who are directly concerned in this country by the implementation of this bill and by its reaction on their daily existence. The number of people who are directly concerned in the regions affected by this bill is as considerable as the number of people in this country who are interested in the automotive industry, and the number of people who are indirectly concerned can be estimated as an aggregate of anywhere between 200,000 and 300,000. A further consideration of the number of people who are vitally concerned in this bill would show that half a million and perhaps 700,000 Canadians have shown their faith in their country and in the mining resources of their country by investing in the various mines which are affected by this bill.
The second reason which would lead me to think the Minister of Finance could have been slightly more generous and could, for instance, have bonused 50 per cent of the basic year production instead of 334 per cent is the fact that the amount involved in either case in proportion to the number of people concerned and in proportion to the purpose of the bill, while not negligible, cannot be looked at as vast under any circumstances. I have already mentioned that perhaps 300,000 people in this country are vitally affected. A great many of them are the more affected because the localities of the regions in which they live exist almost exclusively because of mining operations. It is a fact that of the various regions in this country where mining is conducted, most of them exist also solely because of mining and have become communities, in some

I trust my figures are nearly accurate. I repeat and insist that the Minister of Finance should have been more generous in his attitude toward the mines of this country. However, I do feel that he has taken a step to help and I hope that future legislation will help the mines of this country to survive and attain that prosperity which a great many of them have not , known in recent years.

Gold Mining

It is clearly shown, by a third chart of the Canadian metal mining association that the total dividends paid by Canadian gold mines in 1941 was close to $48,000,000 and in 1947 had sunk to $16,000,000. That should be interesting information for the C.C.F., who seem to think the mines are rolling in wealth. When you realize that their returns have been cut by 300 per cent since 1941 you will appreciate the difficulties they are encountering today.
At the same time I should point out again that nearly all the mining companies have policies whereby they plow back into the mining field a great deal of the revenue they obtain from producing properties.
It struck me that the arguments advanced by the C.C.F. this afternoon were perhaps just as fallacious as they nearly always are in this house. If I might draw a parallel it would be this. They seem to think a man who invents, let us say, a carburetor for your car is entitled to no profit from that invention, but the man who takes the product of his genius and manufactures it into a working model is the one who should get everything. That is the same argument they advance with regard to every other question and it seems to me to be so fallacious that it is about time they gave it up.
I am not going to detain the house much longer, but I wish to say one or two things further about the bill. First, to get back to costs, the cause of the decay in the gold mining industry is the artificial price at which gold is now kept. Until and unless this economically unsound price policy is altered, the gold mining industry will not prosper, and there is no other solution than to permit the industry to find a proper market for its product where the price is not fixed by some other government, or for our own government to sell the product of our mines where it can obtain more revenue in United States dollars, or whatever currency it requires, than it obtains at the present time.
The value of gold to the Canadian economy cannot be over-emphasized. It is to the mining industry and to .the north that we must look for substantial increases in population. Gold has been the incentive for our development as most base metals finds are associated with prospecting for precious metals, particularly gold. It has added tremendously to the stability of our mining operations and it gives flexibility to our operations, which are unique.
Gold is the magnet which draws development. I merely point out as an example of this that Gilbert LaBine was searching for

gold when he found pitchblende and uranium at Great Bear lake. Our agricultural population is showing the tendency of being static, or, in fact, actually declining. If we are to develop, it is to the mines and the PreCambrian shield to which we must look. To suppress artificially the value of the principal product of this rich belt is to strangle the growth of Canada.

I have

It is as the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Skey) has just said. You have heard the expression, once a miner always a miner. That is largely true. In the coal mining business I know it is true that the family gets into mining and stays there. It is certainly true in England.
Then I interrupted and started something I had not intended to start when I asked the leader of the C.C.F. how he would work out this thing, and how it could be done. I asked that question in all seriousness and as yet I have had no answer. I do not think there can be one, for this solid and basic reason. If you take a certain mine which is getting the benefit of this subsidy and its costs are, of course, different from those of other mines in that neighbourhood or in other neighbourhoods, I can see no equitable method whereby you can apply a percentage to go for wages and other benefits, perhaps, without upsetting your whole wage structure and wage scale throughout that industry. That may be possible. The leader of the C.C.F. said that certainly smart people could work it out. May I simply confess that I am not one of those smart people, because I am utterly unable to see how that could be done.
Then we heard something about these wealthy owners. I hope they are wealthy. I am one of those people who are happy when other people make money, even though I cannot do so myself. I could paper the walls of a good big play-room I have in my house with mining shares which I bought and paid for; and they would not even make good wallpaper. That has been my experience in dealing in this business. The answer is, of course, that I have always been a piker; I never had enough money to be anything else. I bought nickel shares, and now they are not worth even that; they are absolutely worthless.
I wish to refer to one matter mentioned by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, namely, this business of workmen's compensation. Like all other developments in labour relations, it has come to what it is now by a process of evolution. In the coal mining business, I remember that many years ago when I was acting for some coal companies I had a fine practice in fighting what we called
workmen's compensation suits. In those days the matter came to what we called the district courts or what you in Ontario would call your county courts. We had lawsuits as to whether or not the person was entitled to compensation. Following that-and I think it is the case in all provinces-boards were set up and the matter was taken from the courts; even the matter of appeal, which I think the mining fraternity now wants returned to them so that they may appeal, was taken over by boards. Those boards then fixed the compensation. I want to disabuse your mind, Mr. Speaker, and the minds of the members of this house of this idea that the companies themselves or the operators themselves have been in any way the enemies of compensation. They simply pay an assessment into a fund, and from that fund come all sums of money

be they lump, be they weekly or be they monthly-which are paid by way of compensation. We will all agree and admit that compensation has been growing from year to year as a part of the evolution and growth of a new idea in these' relationships.
I remember this silicosis business; I remember the men fighting hard to get silicosis in as a compensable disability. I remember at that time seeing figures brought from the coal mines in England. I learned then that the lungs of a coal miner are clear black and stay that way. The medical people, however, do not seem to think that has done him much harm, and they produced figures to show that, in so far as the incidence of tuberculosis was concerned, a coal miner was less affected than a person engaged in, we will say, another occupation, probably a more sedentary one. But that fight was won. Now I believe silicosis is among the compensable disabilities in all provinces of Canada. That battle has been won. I agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South that there are sad cases such as the one he mentioned of the man who in his will gave his body to someone so that his lungs might be examined to prove the existence of the disease, in order that his family might obtain compensation. But we find that in every walk of life; you find it in the Department of Veterans Affairs. You will always find that as long as the minds of men are finite or until medicine and medical men become perfectionists, which of course they never will since they are human beings.
The point I am making is that while there are those odd cases, certainly in the province from which I come, and I have no doubt in Nova Scotia as well, that is not the fault of the employer. He has nothing to do with it; he is completely removed from it. It is a result of the advice given to compensation

boards by specialists. I think, too, that if the hon. member were in his place at this moment he would agree that the experience of workmen who are under compensation is that almost invariably the doubt is resolved in favour of the individual; that is, the employee. I am proud to say that I know this to be true in the province from which I come, and I think it is true in the other provinces as well.
So if when the minister speaks he will give me the assurances for which I asked in the beginning, I will support this bill. But much as I may like subsidies I make this broad statement. In a country of opportunity, equal opportunity-and I think we have approached very close to that position in Canada-subsidies take money earned by one man away from that man and give it to another. That is what they do, in the broad economic picture. Someone may say I am opposed to all subsidies. I am not. Conditions arise, as in this particular case, because of perhaps unusual and extraordinary circumstances, and in such instances I am in favour of subsidies, as I am in favour of this subsidy. Then in so many cases it is found, as I am sure it will be found in this case-and in this I agree with the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Beaudry)-that a subsidy can be regarded as something in the nature of an investment. But I want to take this position, and state it clearly. I do not think there is anything in the argument which has been used here today that because this house is asked to vote a small subsidy for the general good of Canada-because our exchange situation certainly may be to the great detriment of Canada unless we can correct it-we are in any sense taking aw'ay milk from babies or bread from poor people. To my mind that sort of argument is complete and utter nonsense. I know what I have just said will not be popular in many places, but I believe it so thoroughly I had to say it here.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take only a few minutes, but first I should like to correct one statement made this afternoon by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). He said that gold was an essential part of private enterprise. That is not so. Private enterprise is as old as civilization, as old as history itself; the gold standard is quite a modern institution.
I do not want to discuss this bill on technical grounds, but I do want to say that on the most

fundamental grounds I am opposed to the whole idea of gold and the gold standard. If you like, I will put it on religious grounds, I mean religio, to rebind or bind back to reality, truth. Surely it cannot be denied today that millions of people in the world are literally starving to death or in danger of starving to death. Neither can it be denied that the mining of gold is a waste of time, effort and materials at a time when millions are suffering for -want of the bare necessities of life.
If we take the narrow view it may be argued that gold mining is a profitable thing for those engaged in it. If we take the short view it may be admitted that it is profitable for Canada itself. But if we take the long or wide view I think in the end it will be proved that it is not profitable either for those engaged in it or for anybody else.
To say that socialists are opposed to gold and orthodox finance is not borne out by the facts. The London school of economics which certainly would support the gold standard was founded by socialists for the purpose of spreading socialism. I saw just recently that Lord Passfield, one of the founders of the socialist movement in England, was able to accumulate a considerable fortune under the capitalist system and he left that fortune to the London school of economics. Certainly the London school of economics would support gold and the gold standard.
I should like to know how much more gold the world needs. Surely there is enough for the purposes to which it is put today. It is not being coined or used as it used to be used. I can well remember when gold was in circulation, but that is not true today. It is a criminal offence at the present time to have a gold coin in your pocket. Still we are told that we must go on everlastingly mining this stuff which nobody uses and which when it is mined simply disappears into a hole in the ground. Even if we are supporting a gold standard, is it necessary to keep on mining the gold which disappears as soon as it comes out of the ground? Surely the labour, science and materials used in producing gold could be put to better use.
To go on expending this vast effort to produce gold which nobody can use, simply to produce something which it is assumed people must have before they can exchange their wealth, reminds me of what Charles Lamb said about burning the pigsty in order to roast the pig. Surely there is a more economic and convenient way of maintaining a monetary system than continuing this waste of men and materials.

Gold Mining
It can be argued that the future of the men engaged in mining and of the districts in which mining is carried on is bound up in the production of gold, but surely these men could be put to a much more useful task. There are other metals and minerals to be mined, not to mention, as I said before, the production of food of which the greater part of the people of this world are in such need.
Much has been said about inflation, and perhaps when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) speaks he will be good enough to explain why gold mining is not inflationary. It seems to me that it is pure inflation.
The main objection which I have and which I think Social Crediters generally have to a gold standard is that it means the centralization of control. We are opposed to that. We know what happened in 1925 when the gold standard was reimposed. We know the dreadful conditions that were brought about. If a restoration of the gold standard is not intended, then I cannot see the purpose of continuing the mining of gold. It is not used in the arts to any extent and it is not used in our coinage. It seems to me that in the end the real purpose is a return to the old gold standard which I believe was responsible for more misery than any other single institution.
I am not criticizing the policy of bonusing this or that commodity, but if it is a good thing to bonus the production of gold I cannot see why the same principle cannot be applied to any other industry which is in need of support.

They did not use that sort of language in Pontiac or in any gold mining district. I challenge any of these hon. members to go to Pontiac and make the speeches they just made against gold. I know the hon. member for Pontiac cannot relish their viewpoint, but by his silence he seems to agree with them. He never uses those expressions in his own constituency, and he never will. I am positive of that, but he must carry the responsibility of the policies of his party.
We have the Bank of Canada at the present time, which is a government institution. We know that a -monetary system must be resilient; we know that back of the Canadian dollar or of any monetary system you must have the work, you must have the industry, you must have the energy of the people.
The fact that we have treated this subject with intelligence is seen in the results we attained during the war. Who would have dreamed at the beginning of the last war that Canada would be able to finance the war effort which was put forth by the Canadian people at that time? We were able to do so for one primary reason, and that is that parliament realized the elasticity, the resiliency of our monetary system. But it was more than that, for behind the Canadian dollar there were the Canadian people, who put forward the best effort any people have ever made at any time.
I wish to be reasonable on this subject. I was not here this afternoon, but I was told that the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) made as usual a very sensible speech.

speechtext: He always does.

speechtext:
I know he always does, but sometimes people are easily swayed. On one occasion I was told that mine was the golden voice of the gold mining industry. Certainly I can say that the gold mines of this country have proved a fruitful source of employment for our workers, our farmers and those engaged in our forests. That is what gold mining has meant to Canada, and it is one of the finest ways of developing a newer section of the country.
It is easy for anyone to stand up here and fight for the gold mining industry in view of what the industry has accomplished for the country. I do not always agree with all the statements on gold made by the members who
