come from Toronto but I know that they are sincere. I must point out, however, that some of the statements which they made two years ago, at the time the Canadian dollar was brought to a parity with the United States dollar, have not been justified by the events. Those hon. members wanted our gold producers to have access to the world market, to sell their gold on the open market. At that time I stood up in the House of Commons and said that it was impossible for the gold mining industry of Canada to sell gold on the open market of the world.

subtopic: EMERGENCY PAYMENTS TO ASSIST IN MEETING INCREASED COST OF PRODUCTION
speechtext: Why?

subtopic: EMERGENCY PAYMENTS TO ASSIST IN MEETING INCREASED COST OF PRODUCTION
speechtext: Why? The thing is as elementary as ABC. Does the hon. member think for one moment that if the Minister of Finance allowed the gold mining industry to sell its production on the open market the industry would not immediately ask the federal treasury to guarantee the collection of the proceeds from such sales? I leave that question with hon. members.

subtopic: EMERGENCY PAYMENTS TO ASSIST IN MEETING INCREASED COST OF PRODUCTION
speechtext: It would be the same as the wheat industry.

subtopic: EMERGENCY PAYMENTS TO ASSIST IN MEETING INCREASED COST OF PRODUCTION
speechtext:
No, for the simple reason that you are dealing with a different matter. When you are dealing with wheat you know that all the nations of the world want that commodity; but there is only one nation that is willing and ready to buy your bullion at a set cash price, and that is the United States; and are you going to engage in a black market against the United States treasury? That is what it would practically mean. I leave that thought with the hon. gentleman. It would be purely and simply a black market.
Some hon. members have said that as much as $60 an ounce could be obtained for our gold. Let me put this to them, and I am speaking quite sincerely. Suppose tomorrow the Department of Finance allowed the gold industry to sell its bullion on the world market. The next day the industry would be on the minister's doorstep asking, and quite rightly, that he guarantee the collections of the proceeds of those sales, because there would be nothing else for him to do. There is no getting away from that, because these sales would not be made to governments but to individual buyers.
I am not speaking as an expert. I am speaking as a layman, and I believe with common sense, but I have lived in that section of Canada for many years and I know something about the working of the gold mining industry. From such knowledge as I have, I wish to say this wdth reference to the bill
before us, that it is a good measure and a big step in the right direction. I do not suggest that it is perfect, but I would suggest to hon. members that the Department of Finance has always been open-minded so far as the gold mining industry is concerned. Let us be fair. We are all practical men or we should be; if there is one man here who should be practical in regard to this particular question it is myself, and I may say that I could have bitterly attacked the placing of our dollar on a parity with the United States dollar because it hurt the section of the country that I represent here. But the gold mine owners are Canadians and they are good citizens. They knew that the industry was being hurt, but they envisaged the national economy as a whole and they conceded that it was a good thing that the Canadian dollar was being placed at parity with the United States dollar. When the then Minister of Finance, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley), in the month of July, 1946, made his statement in this house with respect to dollar parity he stated at the time that it would harm to some extent the gold industry.
In my constituency there are three large newsprint mills which at present use a little over 3,000 cords of pulpwood per day, and on the night the announcement was made by the then Minister of Finance that our Canadian dollar was at par I received some telephone messages from the management of one of those big mills. I told them not to worry, because the price of newsprint, the price of sulphite, the price of lumber and the price of pulpwood were not all rigidly controlled by the United States treasury, whereas in the case of gold the situation was entirely different. This was so true that it was only a few days later that newsprint increased by $7, $8 and in some instances by $10 a ton.
The gold industry, on the other hand, found itself in a precarious position. But these men in the gold mining industry were fair, even though they had to be critical, and naturally they had to put their case and problems before the public and the government. As I have said, however, they envisaged the national economy as a whole and they did not use the kind of language that was used by some of the so-called mining papers. They *were more reasonable than others that tried to agitate the people, and this is all to their credit. The leading men in the gold mining industry realized that the best and most logical and at the same time the most sincere sort of agitation was to state the facts clearly and forcibly, and to show that the
Gold Mining

gold mining industry deserved careful consideration at the hands of the government as well as at the hands of parliament. The gold mining industry has always played the game, and for that reason these men felt that it deserved every consideration possible and rectification of their position.
When, early in the last war, the federal treasury requested an intensive gold mining production, the gold mining industry of Canada answered at once, without the slightest hesitation, and in doing this it was helping the serious dollar situation in which the country found itself, before we had special agreements with the United States. In many instances they went so far as to deplete their ore reserves, so much so that some of these mines like Hollinger, McIntyre, Lake Shore, and many others for many months and in some cases for a year or two, suffered a depletion of their reserves, which is always a serious situation for a mine. But they did this from a national point of view. They wanted to do all they could to further Canada's war effort.
Two years later, on account of the labour shortage and the shortage of essential metals, they were asked to shift some of their men to employment elsewhere, to the nickel industry at Sudbury, for example, or to the steel industry, and once again the gold mining industry responded magnificently and without any hesitation whatsoever. On that score alone, therefore, I know that the sympathy of the whole of Canada has been behind the gold mining management, and I repeat without fear of contradiction that our gold management has been second to none so far as labour and the working conditions of labour are concerned. It is not perfect; nevertheless it has done some marvelous things.
Here I should like to say something that may perhaps seem to be rather of local interest, but I believe that I am justified in bringing it up because it is also of interest to the nation at large. I may say that our Barbara Ann Scott got her first effective training in the summer months in one of the finest skating rinks in the country, the rink built at Schumacher by the McIntyre mine, to which every worker in the gold mining industry of that section has full access.
In my opinion management in our section of the country has been too humble about what they have done in the matter of health and improved working conditions, et cetera. It should have let the rest of Canada know what was being done for the workers. Unfortunately at times we have had the wrong kind of agitation in our section of the country, where some people have been trying to stir up the population even against their own labour leaders.

Only a few weeks ago the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Gauthier) and the hon. member representing the Temiskaming district and myself pleaded with the government to stop a certain man who was trying to mislead the workers in our section of the country. I could speak of men like the Bickells, the Timmins, the Schumachers, yes, thousands of others that gave their best in its development. Is it because they have taken chances; is it because they have been energetic that they should be penalized? Some started from the ground and worked their way up. No doubt many hon. members listening to me participated last year in a banquet given by the mine managers and operators and everyone who listened to men like Mr. S. L. Longmore, for instance, and other speakers, was impressed with the sincerity of these men, their logic, their comprehension, realizing that they were humanitarians whose one desire was a solid and prosperous industry and peace between labour and management. Every one of these men at that banquet was always at the disposal of the worker to go up and discuss the affairs of the workers with the management. That is one of the best ways to obtain co-operation.
That is why I am in favour of this bill. As I say, it is not perfect, but it is capable of amendment and if necessary of some changes from time to time as new problems arise. When some periodicals say that the government has done nothing for the gold mining industry since 1946 they are not speaking the truth; they are not trying to be fair. Several things have been done and several things have been tried in connection with this important problem. I might point out that I took it upon myself to go to the United States to find out what could be done, what was the situation there. I want the house to realize that United States gold producers are in the same position as our Canadian gold producers. The cost of living has gone up there, as have the wages; also the cost of materials necessary for the exploitation of gold mining is higher in. the United States than it is here at the present time. So when we talk in terms that we should increase the price of gold by $8, $10, or $15 an ounce, we must be very careful indeed.
Some speakers in that group across the floor will say, forget about the United States. They go so far as to say, forget altogether about the gold mining industry; they even wish its destruction. I do not want to see that day come. I hope it will never come. Let us pause and see for a moment what it would mean. In the Porcupine district alone at the present time we have over 75,000 people gainfully employed in gold mining. They have built some fine permanent towns; there are

Gold Mining
some fine schools, and all the public utilities services possible; towns built on permanent lines. There are in northern Quebec, northern Ontario, northern Manitoba and British Columbia, in the gold mining sections of Canada, people from every section of Europe and of Canada working to develop that needed metal for the benefit not only of the section in which they live, but also for the benefit of the whole of Canada.
I could go on indefinitely speaking on this matter. I hope that this summer, if it is at all possible, we may again inaugurate some excursions into northern Ontario and northern Quebec for the members and senators. Two years ago the Ontario mining institute brought, I believe, twenty members of parliament and senators on an educational tour into the Porcupine, Kirkland Lake and Rouyn-Noranda section. For most of them it was their first visit, and they declared that it was a revelation to them. They saw the situation right on the ground.
I am not going to talk politics, but inasmuch as we hear of some people who seem to fear personal initiative and the making of reasonable profits, I am just going to say this. As far as development is concerned, in the initial stages of gold mining more money has been lost than has been made. When you see the work of the prospectors, the promoters, the first engineers and the first men who go into these apparent mud holes, where you have water, even in the summer, right up to your knees, taking a gamble with their own money and that of others-because there will always be a certain amount of gambling attached to it; there is no getting away from that-and working for months and years before they can get a dollar of revenue, and on many occasions meeting with complete disappointment, you must admire their courage, their determination. This is the kind of industry which has enlarged the borders of Canada as a whole, and has pushed back its frontiers. In northern Canada we have a wonderful treasure house. There . used to be a time, even in the section of the country where I live now, when we thought it was not even fit. for the Indians and Eskimos. In the riding which I have the honour to represent now, when I went there in 1909 as a settler in that famous clay belt in the centre of the gold mining section, there were about
1.000	people consisting mostly of Indian trappers, white trappers, and a few prospectors. Today I have the honour and the great responsibility to represent in this house some
140.000	people. That shows the development that we are bound to have in northern Canada, and that applies to nearly every foot of ground of that immense territory. We no
doubt have it to the same extent in the Northwest Territories. We have it to perhaps a large extent in British Columbia.
I am going to make this prophecy. In northern Ontario and in northern Quebec if we are careful with our mining, if we are careful with its development, and if the government and everyone concerned have foresightedness and realize the importance of this industry to the national economy and prosperity of this country, we shall have there the greatest development that any nation has experienced in the last forty years. I know whereof I speak. We hear about the resources of Labrador. The new member from northern Quebec (Mr. Gourd), who so well represents that section of the country, well knows the potentialities they have there in mineral resources. In northern Quebec and northern Ontario we have what we call the wonderful clay belt, one of the most fertile and arable sections of land there is in Canada at present, and that is intermixed with that fine mineral belt. There are no heavy hills. Apparently by glacier action those hills have been erased or rather greatly worn down. There are fine prosperous agricultural communities there. I am going to take the opportunity of mentioning just a few in my own constituency: Raymore, Val Gagne, Cochrane, Fauquier, Kapuskasing, Opasatika, Moonbeam, Mathe-son, Hearst, and many others, all names that hon. members have heard. They have an unlimited regional market in the mining centres. The Montreal, Toronto and other markets are quite far away for us to cover because of the long freight haul. But those regional markets are a wonderful thing in agricultural development. The same thing applies to our forest development, because a lot of timber and lumber is used in mining.
I speak feelingly on this subject, and I know that, I am receiving a fine and comprehensive hearing from every section of the house. Again I repeat what I said a few moments ago. When I was in New York last fall I was happy to read the accounts of the speeches made by the leader of the C.C.F. party when he was in my section of the country. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has also been there. He has done some good work. We know that he is constructive in his labour activities. He wants to do what he thinks is best for the welfare of Canada and for gold mining, because if gold mining is not prosperous or is on a submarginal basis, they cannot pay the wages necessary to be paid to the worker to live eonfortably. When hon. members are, I would not say converted, but convinced of the urgent necessity and the serious problems facing the
Gold Mining

gold mining industry and use their influence accordingly, it will again come into its own. It is not a bankrupt industry but it is in need of practical help. At the present time one may read certain reports, but it is far from being bankrupt. However, it has suffered to a large extent, and it has suffered on account of losing the $3.50 per ounce.
Just one word about subsidies. I know some hon. members of this house will say, Well, you are against a subsidy on milk; you are against the subsidy on this and that, but you are in favour of a subsidy for gold mining. I am not in favour of subsidies for gold mining. I want hon. members to analyse and to judge the situation of gold mining impartially. Is there any other industry in Canada that has suffered as grievously as it did when we put the dollar at parity? I think not. Steel has not suffered in the same way. Neither has nickel. No other mining industry has suffered in the same way or any of our export goods. I repeat that this industry wants to be practical and has proven to be logical. It has no politics, but it realizes the great role that it has to play in the postwar period. The people in my section of the country, the mining interests, would resent it if I had the audacity to make a political speech on this important question. That is why I so highly appreciate the fine attention I have received this evening from every section of the House of Commons. We do not come before parliament as mendicants, hat in hand, for special privileges. We want you to judge the situation impartially and practically. I know if -we unite our efforts we can succeed; that we will succeed in this case.
On the question of maritime rights my section of the country always gave its support 100 per cent. With regard to wheat, you fine farmers in the west will always get support from our section, the mining section of Canada; in all the problems you may have to face, our people, all our section of Canada, will give that support diligently and voluntarily, and we make your problems our problems and naturally we expect, the same favourable support of our difficulties. I believe that under such circumstances we have the right to expect for my section of the country that the problem which means so much not only to us but to the whole of Canada, will be given support and attention and all the study possible so that a solution will be found that will be reasonable to the industry, and will allow it to play its part in our aim for a prosperous and greater and stronger nation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EMERGENCY PAYMENTS TO ASSIST IN MEETING INCREASED COST OF PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it will be necessary for me to make any very extended remarks in closing the debate, but perhaps there are some things I should say. At the outset, however, I believe we have had a useful and helpful debate on the second reading of this bill, in which members on all sides have, I think, made a valuable contribution to a real understanding of the purpose of this legislation.
On December 11 last I made a statement to the house outlining the program the government proposed to recommend by way of assistance to the gold mining industry. That program involved certain modifications of the original proposals I had announced in my broadcast address of November 17. Those modifications, as I stated at the time, had come about following representations which had been made by the gold mining industry, and following consultations which had been carried on with the international monetary fund to which, of course, as a member Canada had certain obligations.
As far as the industry is concerned, the representations made to us were to the effect

Gold Mining
that the original proposal, which was to defray for a three-year period the costs of additional gold production over and above the amounts produced in the base year, which ended December 31, 1947, to the extent of $7 per fine ounce, would not serve to prevent the continued deterioration of the industry and the closing down of additional mines. As far as the international monetary fund was concerned, the consultations were begun immediately after my original announcement, in order to make sure that the detailed working out of the plan was in accordance with our obligations as a member of that organization. In my broadcast I had stated that because of these obligations the details of the program could not be made known until we had discussed them with the fund, and that consequently details would not be made known until I announced them in parliament. But I did indicate in general terms what our proposals were, in order to prevent speculation in the meantime.
In the course of our discussions with the fund it developed that the payment of a fixed dollar amount per extra ounce of gold produced was open, from the point of view of the fund at any rate, to the objection that it might be represented as constituting an increase in the price paid for gold by the government, which, of course, would be contrary to the fund agreement. So in the light of these representations and the consultations to which I have already referred the government decided to modify its proposals, and the general nature of those modified proposals I explained in my statement on December 11. Later, on December 19, when I moved the resolution preceding the introduction of this bill, I elaborated on those proposals.
I do not think it is necessary for me to discuss them now in detail, but when we are in committee we can discuss how those proposals will work out in detail. In view of what has been said during the course of this debate, perhaps I should deal briefly with two general considerations which I consider important in connection with this measure.
In the first place I should like to say a word with respect to its relation to our international obligations. At the end of my statement after moving the resolution on December 19 I placed on Hansard two public announcements made on December 11 by the international monetary fund, following our consultations with them, as well as a statement which had been made the following day by the national advisory council of the United States government. The first statement by the fund attempted to make clear just what the obligations of the member countries are in connection with legislation to subsidize the production of gold. The fund, it was pointed out, has an obligation to see that
the gold policies of its neighbours do not undermine or threaten to undermine exchange stability; and under certain sections of the articles of agreement members of the fund are prohibited from buying gold at a price above parity plus the prescribed margin. In its statement the fund pointed out it was felt that a subsidy in the form of a uniform payment per ounce for all or part of the gold produced in any country would constitute an increase in price which would not be permissible under the fund agreement. In another section of the agreement each member of the fund-
. . . undertakes to collaborate with the fund to promote exchange stability, to maintain orderly exchange arrangements with other-members, and to avoid competitive exchange alterations.
It was felt by the fund that subsidies on gold production would offend against that provision if the subsidies were such as to cast doubt on the uniformity of the monetary value of gold in all member countries, or if they tended to contribute directly or indirectly to monetary instability in other countries. In the light of these two sections of the agreement to which I have referred, our original proposal was found to have objectionable features; and incidentally these provisions of the fund agreement are also the provisions against which allowing a free market for gold or selling gold abroad at premium prices would probably offend.
There were two statements issued the same day. In its second statement the fund made it clear that it had examined the revised Canadian proposal, which is the one incorporated in the bill now before the house, in the light of its general statement of policy to which I have just referred, and had-
. . . determined that in the present circumstances the proposed Canadian action is not inconsistent with the policy stated by the fund.
That statement, I may say, was a matter of gratification to the government in view of the objects and purposes we were seeking to achieve. Before I leave this point we should recognize, and I should like to draw to the attention of the house, the significance of the statement issued by the national advisory council of the United States government. Hon. members will recall that this council consists of the secretary of the treasury, the secretary of state, the secretary of commerce, the chairman of the board of governors of the federal reserve system and the chairman of the board of directors of the export-import bank. On behalf of the United States government the national advisory council welcomed the fund's statement of policy and its expressed intention

speechtext:
That is the statement of cold fact under today's conditions.
The warning contained in the national advisory council's statement against a country becoming too dependent upon subsidized gold production as a solution of exchange problems leads me to the second general point I wish to discuss in closing this debate, namely, the purpose of this legislation.
I do not need to assure the house that, so far as Canada is concerned, there is not very much danger in the contingency referred to by the council, namely, that we shall largely stimulate the production of gold as the result of these subsidies. It is true that the bonus payments we are providing for should lead to some increase in production-I hope they will -but we are not under any illusion that the increased production for this reason alone will be of such magnitude as to become a major factor in the solution of our immediate exchange problems. Any contribution which it makes will, of course, be most helpful, but unfortunately there are other important factors at work which, unless conditions change, will be bound to limit the size of that contribution. I refer particularly to the shortage of labour and the mounting production costs which have been referred to by a number of speakers who have taken part in this debate today.
However, I should like if I may to state the primary purpose of this legislation in somewhat broader terms. Our gold mining industry, as has been pointed out by a number of speakers and without any invidious distinction by my good friend, the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) in particular., occupies a strategic place in our economy, particularly in the development of the social and economic structure in our great northern areas.
As everybody knows, our gold mines are located for the most part in that great mineral bearing area, one of the greatest in the world, which stretches right across the Pre-Cambrian shield in northern Quebec and Ontario, through northern Manitoba and Saskatchewan, up into the Northwest Territories and then down through the mountain area of British Columbia. Many of the mines are small and scattered in remote areas. A good many towns and hamlets have been developed which are solely dependent on them, as are also in certain cases small agricultural communities.
It was the search for gold and other precious metals which was probably the primary factor leading to the discovery of those great mineral areas where the all-important base metals of nickel, copper, lead and zinc and, more recently, the strategic uranium, are produced, with such important results to the wealth and strength
of the country. During the depression years of the thirties gold mining was a powerful factor supporting employment, business activity and the soundness of our international position.
In these and other ways the industry has made an important contribution to our national life. It has been a great dynamic factor in our economic development. By promoting the settlement of our great northern areas it has given the country depth as well as breadth. To us it is synonymous with the north, and I think we all have tremendous faith in the role which the north has still to play in expanding our national wealth and income and promoting our defensive strength.
If that be so, and I think all hon. members will agree with me in that statement, it is important that the industry be maintained in a healthy condition. As I have indicated, during the thirties it was very active and prosperous and its output increased to a peak of approximately $206 million in 1941. That was natural and inevitable. I do not need to tell hon. members that, as long as gold remains directly or indirectly the basis of the monetary standard, it will thrive in depression and languish in periods of prosperity. Its fixed price means that, as costs fall during the downswing of depression the industry's profit margin widens, but as costs again begin their upward climb with the coming of full employment and the boom stage of the cycle the profit margin also narrows and in some cases may disappear entirely.
At the height of the war the necessity of mobilizing labour and essential materials for vital purposes added still further to the industry's difficulties. Production declined steadily after 1941 until the late summer of 1945, and for the year 1945 the output of gold in Canada had fallen to $102,000,000. With the end of the war it was hoped that the industry would before very long be able to get back to its peak production. But while production did pick up to some extent, early expectations were disappointed. The war had brought a more rapid rise in the wages paid by other competing industries and the competition of these industries for labour remained very keen. It therefore proved difficult to rebuild depleted labour ranks and, before long, costs began to rise. Then in July, 1946, came the restoration of the Canadian dollar to parity. May I interject that that action was not only not criticized by anyone to my knowledge, but it was praised and recognized by most as necessary and inevitable. It certainly was not criticized by any hon. gentleman opposite.

speechtext:
I do not recall it, but if the hon. member for York West did, he was the only one. The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Slcey) did not.
An important purpose of this action was to safeguard against a more rapid rise in Canadian costs and prices which would otherwise have been inevitable, but the fact remains that its immediate effect in the case of the gold mining industry was to reduce the price of the industry's product in Canadian dollars roughly from $38.50 to $35 per ounce. Since that date there has been a further substantial increase in wage and other costs.
As a result of all these factors, production in 1946 amounted to only $104 million and in 1947 to $106 million. Much potential production had become or was about to become unprofitable. A number of mines had closed down and a larger number were claimed to be operating at a loss. The closing down of marginal mines not only would bring hardship to many northern communities but would mean in many cases so great a cost to reopen that the mines would probably be lost forever as producing entities. Prospecting for new properties had slowed down and it was increasingly difficult to raise new funds for exploration and development. If this process were to continue unabated, serious damage would be done to the existing social and economic fabric of northern Canada, and the further development of the north would probably be slowed down materially.
This was the type of situation which the government's proposal was designed to remedy, the type of danger it was primarily designed to avoid. The bonus we propose to pay should enable most mines at least to maintain and perhaps to increase their current production to some moderate extent. It should enable many mines to avoid closing down with the hardship this would cause to many communities and the social and economic waste involved in the probable necessary transfer of population and the abandonment of homes and other forms of capital investment.
Those are the main reasons, Mr. Speaker, which prompted the government to take the action which it did. The house will notice that the assistance which it is proposed should

be given is based on half the difference between the fixed figure of $18 per ounce and the actual cost of producing an ounce of gold in the particular mine; this means that it will be particularly helpful in the case of the remote mine and the marginal or high-cost mine. The program should also help to maintain hope and interest and faith in the industiy, make it easier to raise capital, and thus assure the continuance of normal exploration and development work. In other words, it should, we believe, serve to preserve the industry and maintain it in greater health and vigour in a period when rapidly rising costs of production combined with a fixed price were threatening to stifle it. To the extent that the program results in an increased output of gold-and we believe it will to a moderate extent-it will provide a much-needed increase in our reserves of gold and United States dollars. In this connection it is important to note that this contribution will be made without any great increase in the use of our resources, as the gold mining industry is one which is running at only about half its capacity. I do not think there is anything more I need say.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Of course it is not my particular function to state what the long-term policy of the government is with respect to the mining industry. That more appropriately comes within the purview' of my colleague the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen). We have on our statute books and have had for some time, particularly in the tax legislation, special incentive legislation to encourage the gold mining industry. This policy is one which is intended to assist the industry over a temporary period when costs are abnormally high. As to the long-term policy I am not prepared to make a statement now, and I do not think it is appropriate that I should, beyond saying that the dominion government will, as in the past, always be interested in the prosperity and well-being of the gold mining industry, although we do not intend to single out the gold mining industry any more than any other industry for special treatment.
So far as the details of the bill are concerned, I think they can better be dealt with in committee when we are discussing the individual sections of the bill.

May I just say to the Minister of Finance in reply to his statement that no member of the Progressive Conservative party had anything to say in criticism of the government's action on July 5, 1946, I think it is well remembered by many on this side of the house that the hon. member for York West and the hon. member for York South did have considerable to say. It is also very well remembered, by me at least, that four or five days prior to July 5, 1916, the question arose in one form or another in the house, and I made the statement at that time that it was extremely injurious to Canadian business to have the government make arbitrary changes in our exchange rate, and that if the government would leave the exchange rate to its own natural workings we would have a situation with which businessmen could cope and they would not be thrown out of gear so completely as they were on July 5, 1946.
If we consider for a moment just what the circumstances were surrounding July 5, 1946, it will be remembered that OPA, the price control system in the United States, had gone off on July 1 of that year and that a rise in prices was expected in that country. A repercussion of that rise was expected in Canada by a good many people. The cost of living was already higher in the United States that here. Products were cheaper in price, and it was felt that there might be considerable increase in exports from Canada which would deplete our markets and perhaps make it impossible for our government to exercise price control as it was in operation at that time. I well remember this particular matter, because the Ottawa Journal was kind enough to give me a short editorial notice on July 5 and said, if I recall correctly, as its caption, "A prophet in the House of Commons." I clearly indicated that we might expect from the government some change of an arbitrary nature in regard to our exchange rate with the United States; and again, as I pointed out at that time, it was much sounder for the government to leave the exchange rate to the free operation of economic forces rather than to the artificial method which they subsequently adopted and which they have continued to adopt to this day. Businessmen do not know where they are, and I think without question at that time, on July 5, 1946, the Canadian dollar, which had been at ninety cents in relation to the United States dollar, would have improved itself of its own accord without any help from the government. The arbitrary action of the government-

I would at once concede that no operation which would cost for a period of time $50 to produce something that could be sold for only $35 should be continued in existence. But my submission is that in the over-all picture, in view of the large place which the gold mining industry occupies in the Canadian economy, and in view of its tremendous importance to a great many of these scattered1 northern communities, it is desirable as a. temporary measure to give this measure of assistance, first, in order to maintain and perhaps moderately to increase our production of gold, and to improve our exchange reserves and, second, to keep the communities going. Since this is the last clause before we come to the regulations, after which the bill will pass-and I am in favour of iL- I am going to offer a suggestion to the minister. It was advanced to $35 an ounce, but the argument at that time was that the government should have possession of all the gold; that is, that the government should buy all the gold and pay the producer $50 an ounce. The government in turn would sell it at $100 an ounce to those who had to have it. I am not very clear in my recollection of that discussion. I did not get back until six o'clock this evening, and had I known this discussion was coming up I would have refreshed my memory, but it is all in Hansard. Since this is a problem which is very important to the country, I should like the minister to read the debates of those days, because it was Washington and London and Ottawa that advanced the price of gold to $35. It could have been advanced further. Perhaps $35 is not enough. Perhaps it should not be less than $50, or perhaps it should be more than that. The gold industry has a colossal effect on a large number of businesses in Canada, altogether apart from those located in the vicinity of the mines, so that it is almost of transcendent importance. I remember very well the great quantities of machinery and steel which were shipped to northern Ontario following the price advance to $35. I do not know how many mines were opened up; perhaps the hon. member for York South would know, but I believe scores of mines in which the gold ore was low-grade were opened and developed at that time.

That, broke the back of the depression. It was gold that did that. The government gets the credit, of course, but it was the production of gold that bought about such a resurgence of business in all the towns of Ontario and Quebec in which mining machinery and supplies were produced that the depression was finally broken. This looks to me like just a stopgap measure for a while, and in the meantime I suggest that the minister or his officials make an exhaustive survey and at the same time consult with our friends in Washington as to just how much further gold can safely be advanced. It might be possible to pay the producer $50 an ounce, while the government, having possession of all the gold, would be able to sell it at a much higher rate. In those days the argument was that the national debt could be paid off with the money the government received from the sale of gold over and above what it paid the producer, and the amount suggested at that time was $50 an ounce. subtopic: INVESTIGATION, CONCILIATION AND SETTLEMENT OF INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES

speechtext:
Hon. HUMPHREY MITCHELL (Minister of Labour) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a bill respecting industrial relations and investigation of industrial disputes and to make provision therein for the payment out of the consolidated revenue fund of the remuneration and expenses of the members of the boards and commissions and the officers, clerks and employees appointed or engaged by or under the authority of the act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill in question is intended to replace the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act and follow the wartime order
in council, P.C. 1003 of February 17, 1944. The provisions of the bill are almost identical with those of Bill No. 338 which was introduced during the latter part of the session of 1947 and referred to the standing committee on industrial relations after second reading. There are a few minor changes, but nothing of a substantial nature. In order to save time, I would refer hon. members to the statement I made on Bill No. 338 on June 7, 1947, commencing at page 4231 of Hansard.
As I slated in the house at that time, and I have not changed my mind in the meantime, the legislation provides what I consider are the appropriate procedures and conciliation machinery to deal with industrial disputes affecting undertakings over which this parliament has jurisdiction. The essential purpose of the legislation is to create conditions favourable to the free exercise of collective bargaining between employers and employees. For that reason only such regulation of employer and employee activities in their industrial relationship as is considered necessary for the protection of the public interest is incorporated in the legislation. The main responsibility is left with labour and management for the settlement between them of their problems, the negotiation of collective agreements and the administration of such agreements.
The bill will seek to establish an orderly procedure to be observed in the solution and settlement of industrial disputes and it will make available conciliation services to the parties to such disputes. As I stated just now, Bill No. 338 of last session was referred to the industrial relations committee of this house after second reading. That committee held a number of sittings and heard representations from employer and labour organizations and other groups, but it was unable to complete its work on the bill before the prorogation of parliament early in July.
I would point out that the representatives of three out of four of the major labour organizations in Canada who appeared before the committee endorsed the provisions of the bill. I believe I am on sound ground when I say that the employer organizations whose representatives appeared before the committee were reasonably satisfied with the provisions of the bill, although they submitted a number of additional provisions for the consideration of the committee for incorporation in the legislation.
Employer and employee representatives have placed great emphasis on the importance of having uniform legislation in effect in labour
Industrial Relations

relations in industry. I think this is sound and reasonable and sensible. Where you have a uniformity of practice and approach to the solution of labour disputes the trouble is kept, in a comparative sense, at the minimum.
In preparation of Bill No. 338 and in the revisions thereof which are embodied in the legislation which I now propose to introduce, there has been consultation with the provincial authorities with a view to presenting legislation which will be adequate, not only in our own sphere of jurisdiction, but appropriate and acceptable as a basis for provincial legislation. Assuming that the legislation which I am going to introduce is enacted by parliament without any substantial changes, there is, I believe, every indication that the legislation will also be acceptable to a considerable number of the provinces.
Nova Scotia passed a new trade union act in the spring of 1947, which was almost identical in its provisions with Bill No. 338 of last session and with the legislation now being brought down. The Manitoba government has within the last few days brought down before the legislature a new labour relations act, the provisions of which are almost identical with the bill I am now introducing. The minister of labour of Ontario announced in February of this year that, following a study of the proposed dominion legislation, the Ontario government, in the interests of uniform and simplified labour laws, had decided to adopt the proposed dominion legislation. I understand that the province of New Brunswick is studying the dominion legislation before bringing down its own labour legislation. The British Columbia legislation is largely the same as ours with some slight differences. I think it can be fairly said that fundamentally the legislation in existence in Alberta at the moment follows along the same line.
I think it is clearly understood by members of the house that in drafting legislation in the various provinces and the dominion there is bound to be a difference in the language used. In Quebec they always speak of arbitration in referring to what we call conciliation. It is natural that in the provinces of Canada, and I am now speaking of the industrial provinces, there is bound to be some differences in minor matters.

speechtext:
I am glad to-hear my Conservative friends and my good socialist friends applaud that sentiment. That is elementary and fundamental. When you look back to the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act of 1907 you will see that there has been an evolutionary approach to what I believe are sensible and stable labour relations in the dominion, labour relations of the kind and character which, to my way of thinking, compare favourably with those of any country in the world where free institutions exist.
I believe that when you swing too far to the left at one time you are bound to swing to the right the next time. I am one of those who believe that the life of a nation or of civilization moves very much like a pendulum of a clock, swinging backwards and forwards; and to maintain stable labour relations it is far better to go down the middle of the road and to be as fair as is humanly possible both to employer and employee organizations.
My hon. friend the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is smiling, but hp knows what happened in the country to the south of us when the Wagner Act was put on their statute books. Some people thought that it swung too far to the left. They now have the Taft-Hartley law which, in the opinion of some people, is causing a great deal of industrial strife in the United States at the present time. In Australia, where they have a labour government in Queensland, legislation has been passed that swings considerably more to the right than any legislation that exists in the country to the south of us. I do not mention this by way of criticism at all of the people who are charged with responsibility for

Industrial Relations
the administration of affairs in those two parts of the world, because from the very nature of things their legislation must reflect the dominant opinion of the people who sent them to their respective legislatures. Legislators in the United States, Canada and Great Britain, and in New Zealand and Australia naturally all want to be re-elected, so they keep their ear to the ground. The Taft-Hartley law must have been put on the statute book in the United States because conditions existed in that country which the people felt it was necessary to correct, and in Australia somewhat similar conditions must have existed. We too have had our trials and tribulations. That is inevitable when you get two points of view around a council table. If it were not for these honest differences of opinion there woidd be no employer organizations and no trade unions, and that would be a paradise from the point of view of some people. This House of Commons exists as a deliberative assembly simply because there are different points of view in this country, and I hope I shall never live to see the day when some people, perhaps innocently, would like to see persecution substituted for reason in the affairs of this country. Let us be honest and frank and sensible about the matter.
I leave this thought with the house. There is developing in the world today the strike expressly for political purposes. I am not speaking altogether about the Dominion of Canada, but undoubtedly trade unions are being used as an instrument for the destruction of institutions similar to those under which we live. But if we in this dominion travel down the middle of the road, take the moderate course in the establishment and maintenance of labour relations, we shall be making a great contribution to the life of our time. I was taught that you should never pass a law if you cannot enforce it, and we have seen the truth of that in labour relations not only in this country but in other parts of the world. Fundamentally labour relations are based on character, character on the part of the employer organizations and character on the part of the employee organizations. Not all the angels are on the one side. Each has its fair share. I was in the labour movement and I know that we had our fair share of both kinds of human beings. I believe, however, that if we maintain the course on which we have set out we can continue to enjoy comparative industrial harmony in this country. Look the world over and compare conditions with what we have in Canada today. In this country we have only one strike now in progress, and that involves comparatively few people. What other country in the world can 5849-173
say that? It is in my judgment a reflection of the common sense exemplified by both parties in the industrial and trade union life of this country.
I hope that this bill will move with expedition to the industrial relations committee, as suggested by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth).

subtopic: INVESTIGATION, CONCILIATION AND SETTLEMENT OF INDUSTRIAL DISPUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side are in favour of the resolution, treating it as a matter of principle. What we shall say when we see the bill, I do not know. We are told that there are some amendments-we do not know what they are-of the bill that we had last year. But I think I might in a sentence or two affirm two or three principles on the highlights of labour relations in which I believe very firmly, and in large measure I shall speak in agreement with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell).
Across the world I think that in some places mistakes are being made by having too much legislation on labour and industry matters rather than too little. Let me put it in another way. We believe here in collective bargaining. We believe in collective bargaining between industry and strong unions. To say anything else would be a negation of the word "bargaining", because there can be no bargaining in the proper sense of that word if all the strength be on one side of the table. So again I repeat that our principle is that of collective bargaining, but with strong unions. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I must immediately say that I deprecate-I do not know how strongly I can put it-something that has taken place in the province of Prince Edward Island recently where the most backward and reactionary legislation was passed. Talk about the Taft-Hartley act; it is not even to be compared with what they have done in that island on the east coast.
I turn from that to examine briefly one or two principles, because I am anxious to affirm where we stand. There is a word used in labour relations called the "check-off". I want to say that we are strongly in favour of the check-off, and that if it cannot be arranged by collective bargaining I go so far as to say that it should be done by legislation.
The reason the word "check-off"-and it is still criticized and opposed by some very reactionary industrialists, although not many -is disliked by some of our people is the sound of it. It is a harsh-sounding word. It sounds almost Russian. In these days things Russian are not very popular in this country; but to my mind it is just as simple
Industrial Relations

as this. We will say, Mr. Speaker, that I owed you $10 and that you owed the Minister of Labour S10. Then, sir, we will say that you assigned the $10 that I owed you to the minister. In every province of Canada the minister could sue me directly for the money. It is true that perhaps you would need a written notice to sue me, but it could be done. Therefore the employee in an industrial concern is doing nothing more than assigning a portion of his wages to a third party, that party being a union. All this fuss about the opposition to the check-off is, to me, one of the least justified arguments that I know of, because the labour man can do it, anyway, in my opinion, and he can also enforce it. Of course I am referring to the voluntary revocable check-off.
Let me go a step farther. In this case I am going to discuss two or three other things which are agitating people today. One is union security. You cannot just discuss union security; there are so many kinds of it. We have one or two words naming something, and we might be talking about different things and taking our meanings from these words. I am going to say something about strikes. I hope that this parliament will never take from labour its right to strike, but I add this, that some strikes are legal and some are illegal. Never shall we take from any labour organization which is operating under rules-and they are comparatively simple-and has put itself legally in a position of a right to strike, its right to strike; but I think we should, and I hope we shall by legislation outlaw illegal strikes, because we are a country of law-abiding people and we have lived by and have been guided by law.
I want to say another word, and that will be all on this occasion. I refer now to the sympathetic strike. I hope that this parliament and every legislature in Canada will do everything within their powers to outlaw the sympathetic strike. Why? I say that for this reason. You cannot say today that you are in favour of collective bargaining logically and at the same time say that you are in favour of a sympathetic strike. Why? In the sympathetic strike there is no problem between employer and employee. They have no quarrel with one another. Therefore the sympathetic strike becomes what? Not a strike against an employer, but of necessity a strike against the public of Canada, and I hope I will never admit the right of any union the right to do that.
One word more. May I agree with the minister that in other places-and they are not very far away-they have gone too far in trying to legislate certain things. I am not
rilr. Smith (Calgary West).]
going to discuss them in detail. Perhaps it would not even be in good taste to do so. 1 have tried to enumerate two or three principles which I trust will be carried out in this bill which we have not yet seen, and we will reserve our right to discuss the bill more in detail on second reading.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought that perhaps the resolution would pass without discussion, and I did not come prepared to discuss the measure at this stage. I should like, however, to draw the attention of the house to the fact that labour legislation is a live issue today in this country and in the neighbouring country to the south. Generally the tendency in current labour legislation is toward restrictions on organized labour. That is significant, because until recently there has been very little labour legislation in Canada. As I see it, the reason for that was that labour was weak and the employers were strong, and those who were making the laws were not legislating in the interests of labour. That is the situation, and anyone who cares may look up the facts and verify them for himself.
I have been a trade unionist now for almost thirty-eight years. During the whole of that period I have been a member of an organization which had what we called a closed shop. We did not have the check-off as I very well know. Since I was the only paid official of my trade union for some time, I had to go around and see that the members paid their dues. However, if they did not pay their dues we had recourse to the closed shop clause to see that they did. Personally I am in favour of a closed shop or a union shop, whichever term you wish to use, because I do not consider that any employee has any right to wages and conditions which he will not help to maintain. That is not only a policy or the principle that we accept in the trade union movement; it is the principle that we accept in our national and municipal affairs. One may be opposed to paying taxes, but the state says you will pay the taxes whether you are opposed to it or not. Trade union dues are merely a tax that the trade unionist or the employee pays to his trade union for the protection the trade union gives him in maintaining better wages and better working conditions. I could give a striking example of what an employer whom I know thought about the matter and what he thought of the employee who would not pay his union dues.
In regard to this proposed legislation, I am receiving, as I suppose other members of parliament are receiving from chambers of commerce

Industrial Relations
and other employer organizations, resolutions which, if heed were given them, would make of this government, as far at least as organized labour is concerned, a policeman.
One of their proposals is that strike votes must be supervised by the government. Surely trade unionists, members of organized labour, citizens of Canada, should be allowed to decide their own affairs without any supervision from the government, any more than a (private corporation should have the votes of its shareholders supervised by the government. As far as I am concerned, I shall oppose any government supervision of strike votes, or any other kind of votes, so long as the unions themselves can demonstrate that they have control of their union affairs.
There are other questions to which I would like to refer, but I do not think we should have two debates, particularly when the question is to go to the industrial relations committee, where there will be an opportunity to discuss it in detail. However, as regards employers in this country who have opposed labour's every attempt to organize, and anyone who questions that, I would ask him to read the majority report in the labour inquiry of 1943, under the chairmanship of Mr. Justice McTague, the other member of the commission being, I believe, the late Senator Bench.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Labour is merely introducing a resolution to enable him to bring down a bill which has for its purpose the establishing of a national labour code, and I am quite satisfied with that, I will not argue the merits or the demerits of 5849-173i
the bill because I have not seen it. I am a member of the industrial relations committee and I shall examine the bill when it comes before the committee in the light of the proposals that have already been made by the Canadian Congress of Labour.
In my opinion, the Canadian Congress of Labour is a responsible body and it is the legislative centre of the industrial workers of Canada. They have drafted what in their opinion is an adequate measure designed to bring about what the purpose of the present resolution has in view, a national labour code. I do not know what the minister's bill is, but I hope that he and his department have given some study to the proposals made by the Canadian Congress of Labour, because I have read them carefully and I agree with them 100 per cent.
I hope we shall not repeat the performance of last year when we considered Bill No. 338. We sat in the committee a long time and wrangled over it, and I hope the legal minds in the Department of Labour have clarified one point, namely whether we have the right as a parliament to enact a national labour code under the present British North America Act. I hope the minister will be able to tell the committee when it meets whether we can do that, because there is one thing of which I am convinced and of which I think the minister by this time should be convinced, namely, that a national labour code which would embrace the basic industries of the country is absolutely necessary. That was proved to him in the packinghouse workers strike, which occurred in an industry which is established in every province.
You find yourself with a strike on your hands, with meat tied up right across Canada, and you find the federal government powerless to intervene in that strike. You find yourself in the position where the provinces could not get together and come to any sort of uniform understanding.
If a national code is to be effective, then the packinghouse industry should be designated as a national industry and brought under the code, and so should steel. Steel is basic to the economy of the country because it ramifies into every province, and unless these national basic industries are brought under the code it leaves the federal government in the position where, if a general strike takes place in any of these industries, all that the national government can do is to sit back and watch nine little Canadas all jealous of their own prerogatives, refusing to get together, unable to do anything about the matter as a national question, the country being paralysed because there is no legisla-
Industrial Relations

tion to handle the matter. Coal was in that position until the establishment of the national coal board. I believe that under that particular board the federal government has some jurisdiction in the fuel industry.
In the final analysis, labour relations are human relations and there will be difficulties because all legislation cannot be hard and fast. There must be some administrative latitude, some give and take. I have some definite opinions on some of the matters touched upon tonight, and I would be wasting my time and the time of the house if I went into them, because the place where that can properly be done is when the bill is brought down and I have been able to examine it and to discuss it clause by clause with a view to developing the proper mechanics.	.
One thing I would ask the minister to do when the committee sits is to answer the question whether we have jurisdiction under the British North America Act to enact a national labour code, and, second, whether we are prepared to designate basic national industries running from coast to coast as national industries that can be brought under the code, so that the minister may not be faced with a crisis some time in the future where there is a general strike in one of the industries and he is powerless to do anything about it.

speechtext:
The resolution precedes the introduction of a bill to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act, with which I think all hon. members are quite familiar. In the main it is the purpose of the bill to improve the amounts payable to the beneficiaries under that legislation. Hon. members will realize that practically all those beneficiaries are veterans of world war I. In recent years my department and this house have quite properly given a great deal of attention by way of legislation to the new veterans of world war II. The old veteran has not been forgotten with respect to pensions and other matters, but there is a desire here to improve the condition of those vho are, in the main, unemployable.
Since this legislation was first introduced in 1930 its objective has been to give the federal .authority the right to provide assistance to those veterans who fought in the first war, and who are to some extent unemployable. In the main this bill is designed to increase the amounts payable to them, and to deal with other subsidiary matters indicated in the resolution.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.
